html:
I watched the excavator eat into my childhood home one bright fall. Its steely fangs bit into the cedar my father had nailed in more than four decades earlier. Windows burst inward. A slanted roof buckled. One wall heaved before folding into another, disappearing in plumes of sawdust, glass and sheetrock.

I expected grief. I awaited a distinctive pain that comes only from watching the place that held your formative memories disappear into a pile of timber and insulation. But instead, I felt relief. Watching the structure come down meant seeing the building that organised my inner life begin to fade.

My father called the house a refugee. He meant it as a joke, though not entirely. Like him, it appeared foreign in a town where families had lived for generations. Built on pilings above the marshes of Broad Channel, a narrow island in Jamaica Bay on the edge of New York City, it looked as though it landed there by chance.

He built it in the early 1980s after spotting a burned-out lot on his way to Rockaway Beach. Where others saw a charred garage and overgrown, wheat-coloured grass, he saw possibility.

Soon, he recruited fellow eastern European immigrants and paid them in cash, six-packs of Coors Extra Gold and Marlboros. Together, they built a three-storey house with a slanted roof.

Nothing was quite straight. Tiles never lined up. Rain always found a way inside. During winter, without central heating, rooms warmed only with space heaters while elsewhere you could see your breath. The house squealed in high winds and shivered through nor’easters.

We retreated upstairs as if on a lifeboat while the house swayed on its pilings

The birdhouse-like structure was never beautiful, but it was well-constructed and refused to surrender to its surrounding elements. Whenever a big storm hit, it proved its strength.

My father fit this same resilient archetype.

He’d spent his earliest years moving through refugee camps in postwar Germany after his family fled what is now western Ukraine. His six brothers and sisters moved through seven refugee camps in five years. They slept in divided classrooms as ‘displaced persons’. My father grew used to hunger while his parents struggled to survive. My grandmother, Kunegunda, would smuggle her silverware into each camp while my grandfather, Ignacy, would cradle his vodka-bootlegging gear as a moveable business. They both held on to what little they could, convinced they might have to leave again tomorrow.

The United States promised a stability my father’s family had never known. Yet he never trusted this belief. Ever since arriving in the US, he relied on chaos over peace, endurance instead of comfort. The house he built reflected this mindset.

During one nor’ easter in the early 1990s, bay water flooded the first floor of the house while wailing winds rattled the windows so violently I thought they would implode. We retreated upstairs as if on a lifeboat while the house swayed on its pilings. Long after the storm passed, I lay awake listening to the building judder in the darkness.

Looking back, the house came with two competing realities: it showed me wonder while teaching me to expect instability.

I remember the seasons most. In summer, the home became a treehouse hovering over the lapping water. My sister and I fed swans, netted blue crabs, and learned to windsurf. In winter, we laced on skates and crossed the frozen channel to the nearby Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge where we spotted greater snow geese with our golden retriever, Blondie, slipping and sliding his way along the ice.

When my sister and I returned from our winter adventures, my mother made us hot chocolate while my father poured himself a vodka. My mom drank wine and played Simon and Garfunkel’s live concert from Central Park on the tape deck as we sat thawing by the fireplace.

The place felt alive and I loved it severely. It also felt as though it might come apart at any moment and riddled me with worry

‘This is Xanadu,’ my father liked to say. On the rickety, water-warped dock overlooking the bay, he would insist: ‘You can travel anywhere from here.’

The entire place felt alive and I loved it severely.

It also felt as though it might come apart at any moment and riddled me with worry.

Years later, the writer Andrew Solomon put words to what I felt. ‘Nirvana occurs when you not only look forward to rapture, but also gaze back into the times of anguish and find in them the seeds of your joy,’ he wrote in Far from the Tree: Parents, Children and the Search for Identity (2012). ‘You may not have felt that happiness at the time, but in retrospect it is incontrovertible.’

My mother tried to make the house feel steadier than it was. She’d grown up in Montreal, had studied art, travelled widely, and met my father by chance in Mexico while sailing from Portugal. She filled the crooked rooms with colour, music and food from places my father only imagined visiting. She introduced me to Nina Simone, French, and Campari. She rolled sushi on the kitchen counter, and painted the walls in vivid shades while my father disappeared with his brother to hunt in Connecticut. Whenever he embraced disorder, she responded with a cool serenity.

On Friday nights, after I started university, I would take the A-train from Manhattan to see my father. We’d sit by the fireplace drinking vodka while the cherry wood snapped over old newspaper in the fire. A cigarillo rested between his fingers, filling the room with its sweet and bitter scent.

One winter evening, he stared into the flames longer than usual.

‘My father wanted to get rid of me,’ he said.

A story followed about him being sick on a train in Germany while transferring camps. His father thought an unhealthy child would end their chances of emigrating, but his mother saved him from being thrown off the train. It was the closest I ever saw him to crying.

Compared with his childhood, mine was easy. But kids don’t compare their lives with history they didn’t live through. They compare it with their homes.

My family’s breaking point came during that first year of college. My mother had been diagnosed with breast cancer. On Christmas Eve, an argument erupted that ended with a shattered glass table. Pierogies slid across the floor. Wine-hued borscht bled into the carpet. Before midnight, my mother packed her things and left.

I knelt on the floor gathering shards of glass while my father sat near the fire, a cigarillo glowing between his fingers.

Without looking at me, he said: ‘Your mother wanted to throw you in the garbage when you were born.’

The words felt pent up and and arrived like a gut punch.

Pain like this can change form but often carries import for years. Psychologists now recognise that trauma can even extend beyond a single lifetime. This transmission occurs through emotional patterns and parenting styles. It can happen in the way a man treats his home and those who reside within it. It can transpire in how he transfers pain to his own child.

I didn’t recognise I was still staring through the scuffed-up windows of my father’s house

Looking back, I’m not sure if he was trying to wound me as much as connect. The rejection he felt as a child had become part of a dialogue through which he was forced to understand love, disappointment and family. He handed me a pain that voyaged across generations. It journeyed through wars, triumphs and tragedies until it landed near a shattered dinner table in Queens that Christmas Eve.

I visited, I awaited the worst, even when nothing happened. I mistook frenzied caution for astute awareness. I thought staying alert could prevent the next disaster. Over time, such experiences can produce what psychologists call hypervigilance, a heightened sensitivity to threat. The neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett has described the brain as a prediction organ, continually using past experiences to anticipate what will come next. Environments play a central role. At home, I was always on the lookout for the next calamity or volatile indiscretion. This habit would follow me for years after leaving Broad Channel. I expected relationships to fracture, success to dissolve, good fortune to reverse. Moments of happiness often carried a wary mistrust. I assumed this was a clear view of the world. What I didn’t recognise was I was still staring through the scuffed-up windows of my father’s house.

Wedged between Howard Beach and the Rockaways, Broad Channel existed in a perpetual negotiation with its surrounding waters that acted as both a threat and a neighbour. Every storm seemed capable of redrawing the map; every stunning sunset promised a celebration for the eyes.

When Hurricane Sandy tore through the island in 2012, things changed. Five feet of saltwater poured into my father’s house. The dock splintered. Furniture floated before setting into a thick grey sludge. I drove to the island first as a journalist covering the storm and then as a son trying to salvage what remained, carrying waterlogged boxes to the curb, and rescuing family photos.

The house had survived again but there was a shift. Around the same time, my father’s health began to fail. A quintuple bypass became stents that turned to medications he resisted taking. Slowly, a frailer version of the man who’d once built an impossible house with his own hands would greet me when I visited.

The room where Christmas exploded was gone. I stood where the fireplace once was

Buckets appeared beneath new leaks, instead of caulking. Shingles went unreplaced. Whenever I did work on the house, I would come back to see more leaks and more lost shingles to replace. Both the house and the man seemed engaged in a battle with time and its environmental pressures. Both refusing to surrender, and each losing more ground each day.

My father died of heart failure in late 2023. The house sat empty through a lengthy probate while vandals stripped the home of copper wiring, smashing windows and looting what they could. After years of storm damage, the city deemed it unsafe and ordered an emergency demolition.

Two years later, the house still stood, hovering defiantly over the bay even as it was getting torn down.

I gripped a cigarillo like the ones my father smoked. While the house broke off in pieces, I saw Blondie barking at the snow geese. My mother laughing at the bright yellow she painted the kitchen. My sister and I balling bagel dough to feed swans. My father shirtless telling stories of Germany from his water-logged Xanadu.

By late afternoon, there was nothing left of the structure except industrial trash heaps full of memories. The room where Christmas exploded was gone. I stood where the fireplace once was. The marsh had grown peaceful. Without the house, Jamaica Bay seemed larger, as if the horizon zoomed in.

I waited for the familiar tightness in the chest, the racing of the mind. I lit the cigarillo. The tide was about to rise again across the marsh. Planes climbed into the chalky blue sky from JFK. I paused for heartache but something else came. I rolled my shoulders, exhaled a cloud of smoke, and felt an unexpected release.

As the sun hovered, for the first time I could remember, I wasn’t bracing for the next storm.
